name: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content

lead: Glow-up content is the genre of before-and-after videos and posts showing someone's changed appearance, often crediting skincare, fitness, grooming, clothing or procedures. Viewers use them as examples of what is possible and as templates for their own changes.

The chain is seeing the before-and-after, learning the methods credited, then copying changes to your own looks. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which has long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film. Few published sources study social-media transformation content specifically.

paras: People watch or save transformation posts, note the haircut, skincare routine, clothing or training approach credited, and try them. Many also post their own progress photos to track and share changes over time.

Before-and-after posts are selected and edited, so lighting, angles and timing can account for part of the difference. Related research links social-media exposure to appearance comparison, so some people find the genre motivating and others find it discouraging.

angle.text: Transformation videos and posts show before-and-after changes in clothing, haircuts, skin, fitness or procedures, and viewers use them as templates and motivation for their own changes. The genre is popular; few studies examine it.

lead: Self-improvement 'glow-up' content refers to transformation videos and posts that present a before-and-after change in appearance, usually with the methods credited, such as skincare, grooming, fitness, style changes or cosmetic procedures. Viewers use it as a source of ideas and examples for their own appearance goals, and creators use it to document and share their progress. It is a social-media descendant of the makeover genre, which Wikipedia describes as a radical change in appearance involving clothing, haircuts, cosmetics and sometimes weight loss, plastic surgery or dental work.[1]

Makeovers have long featured in daytime talk shows, personal makeover television series and film.[1] Virtual makeover apps now let users preview cosmetics, hairstyles and eyewear on a photo or through a phone camera in real time.[1] Wikipedia's makeover article does not cover social-media transformation content or research on it.[1]

Researchers have studied how before-and-after images on Instagram and TikTok influence people considering cosmetic treatment, with reviews describing educational benefits alongside concerns about unrealistic expectations.[2][3]
infobox: Before-and-after videos, photo comparisons, progress updates

paras: Makeover television formats listed on Wikipedia include Queer Eye, What Not to Wear, Extreme Makeover and Pimp My Ride, and makeover plots recur in films such as My Fair Lady, Clueless, Mean Girls and The Devil Wears Prada.[1] Makeovers are usually viewed positively, as a way to start fresh or improve one's life.[1]

A 2026 narrative review reports that Instagram and TikTok drive interest in whitening, veneers and orthodontics, finding educational benefits alongside unrealistic expectations and misleading before-and-after images.[2]

A 2026 cross-sectional study of 500 adults in Saudi Arabia having upper eyelid surgery found that 88 percent reported some social media influence and that before-and-after images were the most influential content, cited by 64 percent; strong influence was associated with slightly lower three-month satisfaction, mainly linked to recovery expectations.[3]

A 2026 scoping review of 58 studies reported that appearance-focused social media use is consistently linked to body dissatisfaction and body surveillance in adolescent girls and young women, and that body-positive and body-neutral content appeared most protective.[4] A 2026 randomised trial of 150 young women found that viewing fitspiration TikTok videos increased social comparison, appearance concerns and sadness compared with control content.[5] These studies concern appearance-focused content generally rather than transformation posts specifically.
No studies found on transformation content as a genre. Related research on social media, before-and-after images and body image is summarised above.[2][3][4][5]
